How Transformers Attend — Part I

🏷️ Machine learning · mathematical analysis of attention measurements

Carles Marín

At a glance

Part I collects five theorems and two propositions in the main text, eight calibration and bound theorems in Appendix K, six definitions and one empirical conjecture. The Isabelle proofs cover eight groups of the appendix; Lean verifies parts of four main-text results. None of these proofs establishes how a model is trained.

📐 Setting (from the paper, Section 1.4)

Within the normalized family, larger \(\gamma \) shifts mass toward shorter distances. For a general model, a fitted \(\widehat\gamma \) describes only the profile and interval on which it was estimated. A configuration value \(\gamma _P\) is a separate candidate. The exploratory five-axis regression in Section 5.5, with reported \(R^2=0.44\), describes the initial panel; its coefficients do not identify separate causal contributions.

Corrected English edition: formal results integrated, 19 November 2026

Known algebraic, numerical, implementation-description and cross-reference errors identified in the audit are corrected in this edition. Unsupported physical identifications and performance guarantees have been withdrawn. Superseded prose, tables and controller code remain in the separate source archive; they are not reproduced as an alternative set of conclusions here. Appendix J records the resolutions. A new reference implementation repairs prefix causality, head-projection placement, rotary pairing and the context-input interface, with synthetic checks described in Section 19.3. Those checks do not replace the archived model results or establish trained-model efficacy. Unavailable historical observations are identified as missing evidence; no values have been invented to fill them. Appendix K adds eight groups of mathematical results with their verified Isabelle/HOL proofs and explicit hypotheses.

Abstract.

A measured profile and a conditional mathematical family. This corrected edition studies attention-distance profiles, the finite power-law family \(p_\gamma (d)=d^{-\gamma }/Z_N(\gamma )\), and the applications originally proposed within the Thermodynamic Attention Framework (TAF). It preserves the original subject matter and detailed evidence while correcting the inference from rotary geometry to a universal trained exponent. RoPE gives an exact sine–cosine score decomposition. It does not, without further assumptions on learned queries and keys, impose a log-distance expectation or the maximum-entropy principle. The proposed configuration formula \(\gamma _P=(2\theta -T\sqrt2)/(2\theta +T\sqrt2)\) remains an algebraic candidate; its stationary-phase derivation is withdrawn because an essential logarithmic ratio equals \(-1\) rather than the proposed variable exponent.

Instrument dependence. The initial E4 procedure changes sequence length with distance. Its actual extractor returns \(\widehat\gamma =0.782582\) with \(R^2=0.988452\) on uniform causal attention over the seven-point 30–2000 grid. Thus a good power-law fit does not identify learned decay or validate the Padé candidate. In contrast, the audited October QL estimator uses fixed query positions and has zero uniform-null slope on its fitted range. These are synthetic instrument checks, not new model measurements. The initial and October protocols remain distinct.

Coordinate and field controls. The available B3 masks remove unequal sets of adjacent coordinates, not complementary rotary planes. The GPU amplification code also modifies V. The separate field estimator uses \(d+60\) tokens and gives a uniform-null slope \(0.755252\), close to the initial checkpoint’s \(0.757234\). Archived effects therefore do not establish a learned geometric optimum, semantic reservoir or functional interpretation of the spectral ratio.

Empirical record and its update. The original model panels, corpus contrasts, ablations and negative results are retained with their historical status. The selected-case accuracy statistic is withdrawn because its row membership and selection record could not be reconstructed (Section 5.4). A saved-data replay reconstructs October fits and sequence-bootstrap intervals for 25 of 42 historical model identifiers: 15 at context 2048 and ten at 1024; 17 have no recovered observation. The historical text exponent falls inside the corresponding interval in one of 25 cases. Spearman correlation is \(0.269\) between historical and QL exponents, and \(-0.445\) between 19 stored Padé values and QL exponents. Changes in corpus, precision and protocol prevent assigning all discrepancies to one cause. Only four successful job records contain an immutable weight revision. Replaying arrays is not an end-to-end replication of inference.

Mathematics retained with explicit hypotheses. On a finite discrete support, maximum entropy at an interior prescribed log-distance moment has a unique power-law optimizer with a real exponent. Positivity requires the moment to lie below its uniform-distribution value. Exact finite sums determine the normalizer, entropy, Fisher information and formal heat capacity. The continuous variance \((\log N)^2/12\) at \(\gamma =1\) is not the discrete value: at \(N=2000\) they are \(4.81448\) and \(5.48412\), respectively. The Fisher metric obeys \(C_V=\gamma ^2I\); the intrinsic length integrates \(\sqrt I\), and the two quantities need not peak together. The finite continuous mass quantile is well defined on both sides of one, with value \(N^f\) at one; the token-distance quantile instead uses partial sums.

Applications and limits. The compression experiments, context-extension tests, per-head profiles, alignment comparisons, circuit hypotheses and architectural descriptions remain available in their original sections. A frozen-row output error can be bounded from removed mass and value diameter, but that bound does not certify autoregressive task accuracy. Inverse Padé returns its input context exactly and therefore cannot independently validate a retrieval horizon. Divergence from a normalized positional null does not by itself identify a circuit. Geometric band counts require the actual rotary subspace and pairing convention; completion of a cycle does not establish loss of information. The remaining analogy and score definitions have explicit domains and no claimed physical identification or calibrated predictive interpretation. The corrected intervention reference is distinguished from the defective historical implementations and their archived aggregate scores.

The November campaign adds 8,064 saved interventions on 32 shared prompts for three models. The reported gradient-prediction gains concern error prediction, not improved model capability. Appendix K integrates eight formally verified groups on instrument nulls, affine exposure, mixtures, quantiles, finite-family sensitivity, truncation, softmax and the conditional RoPE approximation. Their proofs establish the stated mathematical implications, not the empirical pipeline or bibliographic novelty. The companion Blueprint maps the statements, proofs, figures and interactive calculations of this edition. TAF Agent and the field guide provide application and measurement routes; their outputs are not independent validation of the empirical claims.

1 Introduction

1.1 An Empirical Regularity

Measurement qualification.

The initial empirical pattern must be read with the instrument control in Section 9.1. Under its variable-length sampling rule, uniform causal attention already gives a fitted exponent near \(0.78\). The pattern alone does not establish learned decay, a rotary mechanism or a universal exponent. Fixed-query QL uses a different null and protocol.

Attention-distance profiles summarize how a model distributes attention over token separations under a specified corpus, context and estimator. The family

\begin{equation} A(d)\; \propto \; d^{-\gamma } \tag {1} \end{equation}
1

provides a compact description of some such profiles. Its adequacy is an empirical question: an arbitrary softmax of learned dot products need not have this form. A high log-log \(R^2\) on a selected distance interval does not establish the same law at attention sinks, at every head, or outside that interval.

The initial model panel spans Pythia-14M to BLOOM-7b1 and includes RoPE, ALiBi and learned positional encodings. In the replayed 21-row panel, P03, P05 and P07 have \(R^2{\lt}0.95\); the other 18 exceed it. This panel motivated the configuration-only candidate studied in Section 5, whose accuracy must be assessed on an explicitly identified set of observations. Corpus, precision, architecture, training and measurement choices must be considered when comparing fitted exponents.

The saved October measurements supply a second, explicitly defined comparison (Section 8). Fits and sequence-bootstrap intervals can be recomputed for 25 of 42 model identifiers: 15 at context 2048 and ten at 1024. Seventeen identifiers lack recovered observations. One of the 25 initial text exponents lies in the corresponding interval. The Spearman correlations are \(0.269\) between initial and recomputed exponents and \(-0.445\) between 19 stored Padé values and recomputed exponents. These comparisons demonstrate sensitivity to the measurement protocol; because several conditions changed together, they do not identify a single causal source of the differences. Only four successful job records identify an immutable weight revision. Recomputing saved arrays therefore verifies the reported calculations, not the entire inference pipeline.

One-line summary.

We measure distance profiles, analyze a conditional finite power-law family, and test specific interventions. The geometric description, the mathematical family and the empirical response are connected by explicit hypotheses and comparisons, rather than by an assumed universal exponent.

1.2 Four Questions

  1. Why consider a power law? For a prescribed feasible log-distance moment on finite support, maximum entropy selects a power law. Whether measured attention meets this optimization premise requires evidence.

  2. What determines \(\gamma \)? A measured exponent depends on the model and protocol. We compare it with a configuration-based Padé candidate; RoPE alone does not derive their equality.

  3. What is special about \(\gamma =1\)? It separates the summability regimes of the infinite-support family. At any finite context the normalizer, entropy and variance remain finite and smooth. Continuous and discrete quantiles must be distinguished.

  4. What can we do with \(\gamma \)? Profiles and conditional bounds can guide compression, context-extension and anomaly experiments. Task-level benefits must be measured under the intervention actually performed.

1.3 The Theoretical Chain

The argument starts with three separate objects. First, RoPE supplies a set of rotation frequencies and an exact sine–cosine decomposition of attention scores. Second, a specified log-distance moment defines a constrained inference problem. Third, measurements determine whether a particular trained model is described adequately by the resulting family.

For integer \(N{\gt}1\) and an interior feasible moment \(0{\lt}\lambda {\lt}\log N\), maximizing Shannon entropy over distributions on \(\{ 1,\ldots ,N\} \) with \(\mathbb E_p[\log d]=\lambda \) selects a unique power law. Its exponent is a real Lagrange multiplier, positive only below the uniform log moment \(\log (N!)/N\). The Gibbs-inequality argument and the precise hypotheses are given in Section 6. Other distributions can share the prescribed moment without maximizing entropy. The frequency geometry does not impose either the moment or the optimization principle on trained queries and keys.

This distinction also limits the proposed geometric prediction. A rational function of configuration variables can be evaluated without inference, but that computational convenience does not make it a derived trained exponent. Section 5 analyzes the candidate, the unsuccessful derivation and the empirical comparisons separately. All downstream uses retain this boundary.

1.4 The Central Object

Within the normalized family, larger \(\gamma \) shifts mass toward shorter distances. For a general model, a fitted \(\widehat\gamma \) describes only the profile and interval on which it was estimated. A configuration value \(\gamma _P\) is a separate candidate. The exploratory five-axis regression in Section 5.5, with reported \(R^2=0.44\), describes the initial panel; its coefficients do not identify separate causal contributions.

The geometric quantity is the number of rotary planes that have completed a cycle. For \(m=d_{\rm rot}/2\), \(d{\gt}0\) and \(\theta {\gt}1\), define

\begin{equation} \boxed {\; n_\mathrm {active}(d)=m-k_c(d),\qquad k_c(d)=\min \! \left\{ m,\max \! \left\{ 0,1+ \left\lfloor m\frac{\log (d/2\pi )}{\log \theta }\right\rfloor \right\} \right\} .\; } \tag {2} \end{equation}
2

Here \(n_\mathrm {active}\) counts planes without a complete cycle, not information-bearing dimensions. The actual rotary subspace and coordinate pairing must be used. The continuous logarithmic count is an approximation to this integer count; it does not supply a trained attention exponent or an information-loss theorem.

1.5 The Many Faces of \(\gamma \)

The notation must distinguish quantities whose equality is not established.

Quantity

Meaning and scope

\(\widehat\gamma \)

Estimated profile exponent, with protocol and uncertainty.

\(\gamma \)

Parameter of the finite probability family; identities are conditional on this model.

\(\gamma _P\)

Rational candidate computed from configuration, requiring empirical comparison.

\(1/\gamma \)

Formal inverse-temperature coordinate when \(\gamma \ne 0\), not the output sampling temperature.

Architecture fingerprints are statistics formed from these quantities. Their diagnostic usefulness depends on the reference panel and validation protocol.

1.6 What This Paper Contributes

The paper develops the following connected analyses. Mathematical statements, derived calculations, model measurements and proposals carry different evidence.

  1. Configuration candidate and its limits (Section 5). Building on measured attention-distance structure criticalattn2025,barbero2024roundandround, we analyze \(\gamma _P=(2\theta -T\sqrt2)/(2\theta +T\sqrt2)\), including its domain, inverse, comparison panel and failed stationary-phase argument. The initial comparison identifies all 13 computable residuals; the October comparison uses its own protocol.

  2. Conditional maximum entropy (Section 6). We specify the support, reference measure and feasible moment, derive the optimizing family, and distinguish its entropy \(S=\log Z+\gamma \mathbb E[\log d]\) from measured attention entropy.

  3. Finite and asymptotic regimes (Section 7). Exact sums separate finite-context calculations from infinite-support limits and continuous approximations. Comparisons of compressibility between models remain observations, not universal ratios.

  4. KV compression (Section 11). We derive continuous and discrete mass windows and a frozen-row output bound. The experiments retain the windows actually tested: EXP-B2 used 445 tokens for Pythia-1B and 1482 for Pythia-2.8B. The soft-decay comparison favors different policies on its three models; its percentages depend on the stated denominator. The unsuccessful cases remain part of the evidence, and none establishes general accuracy guarantees.

  5. Context extension (Section 12). EXP-B1v5 compares four Pythia models at \(\alpha \in \{ 1,4,8,16\} \) and nominal lengths 512–4096. At 4096, \(\alpha =4\) scores \(86,100,100,100\% \) in restricted key ranking. It does not dominate every setting and incurs small recorded short-context losses on Pythia-70M. The small-model panel duplicates v4; nominal chance is not a measured control. Neither an optimum nor fine-tuning performance follows from these aggregates.

  6. Entropy and band interventions (Sections 7.4 and 13). The finite entropy bound is mathematical; the replayed finite-family calculations are tabulated in Section 8. EXP-B3 reported perplexity increases of 350 and 9.3 on Pythia-1B for two sets of ablated weight rows. The ratio from the unrounded records is \(37.45\) (approximately \(37\times \)). This contrast motivates a band hypothesis, whose causal interpretation requires correct pairing and partial-RoPE controls.

  7. Attention anomalies (Section 14). Divergence from a normalized positional reference identifies departures from that reference. Circuit identification additionally requires functional interventions.

  8. Measurement workflow and model panels (Sections 9 and 17). The model tables, measurement software and protocol records support reproducible comparisons. Available and missing observations are reported explicitly.

  9. Control proposals (Sections 3 and 19). We separate RoPE changes, score temperature, training and output sampling. The proposed bands below \(0.65\), from \(0.65\) to \(0.85\), and above \(0.85\) are exploratory design choices. A thermostat requires prospective task evaluation.

  10. Information geometry and physical analogies (Sections 7.3 and 20). The finite-family identity \(C_V=\gamma ^2 I\) and rational-map derivatives have explicit mathematical domains. Fractional-operator, conformal and renormalization interpretations are assessed against the additional structures they would require.

  11. Intervention evidence (Section 19.2). The adaptive historical hooks fail prefix causality; their reported scores and the former Fisher recovery comparison cannot validate causal performance. The November campaign supplies 8,064 interventions on 32 shared prompts for three models, including controls and paired uncertainty. Predictor-error reductions are not improvements in model capability.

  12. Failure analysis (Section 20.9 and Appendix F). The proposed geometric hallucination scores lack factual-error calibration. Their domain failures and the unsuccessful controller and physical hypotheses delimit what the framework can support.

Reader’s map.

Sections 5–7 separate candidate geometry from conditional mathematics; Section 8 presents the measurement panels and replay. Sections 11–12 and 19 contain intervention applications. The diagnostics, architecture comparisons and software descriptions retain their detailed methods and examples. The formula catalogue and compendium organize the results with their domains; the separate change and evidence document records version history and the exact scope of formal certificates.

1.7 Relation to Prior Work

Attention profiles and rotary geometry.

Work on attention-distance structure and rotary representations criticalattn2025,barbero2024roundandround,attngravity2026,su2024roformer provides context for the profile measurements examined here. This manuscript does not establish a first-principles exponent for learned attention. Its conditional maximum-entropy result and configuration candidate have different premises and must be assessed separately from the empirical fits.

Context extension.

The context-extension literature studies rotary schedules and extrapolation yang2024understanding,ropebounds2024,ropedimension2025,ropemodulation2026,peng2023yarn,liu2023scaling. Hybrid positional schemes and rotary-dimension analyses provide further comparisons ropenopebackagain2025,shang2025rcdim. Inverting our candidate does not derive the optimal parameters of these methods or identify which layers can discard rotary information. Section 12 gives the precise inverse and separates it from the recorded retrieval experiments.

KV-cache compression.

SnapKV, H2O, StreamingLLM and PyramidKV use different selection or allocation mechanisms snapkv2024,zhang2023h2o,xiao2023streamingllm,cai2024pyramidkv. BLASST and reasoning-focused evaluations offer additional empirical comparisons blasst2025,holdontothat2025. Related compression and layer-skipping work includes mixcompressrefine2025,shortgpt2024,csordas2025layerskipping,elitekv2025. These methods do not all implement a distance-window quantile. Our conditional mass budget therefore does not explain a universal operating point or replace their calibration. In particular, the previously asserted BLASST coefficient and PyramidKV retention match were incorrect; the corrected algebra and numerical comparison are in Section 11.4.

Positional diagnostics and circuits.

Studies of positional and symbolic attention deconstructpositional2025,decouplepsymbolic2025,barbero2024roundandround motivate hypotheses about rotary bands. Here the observed band-ablation asymmetry is retained, with instrument limitations, rather than presented as a proof of a semantic reservoir. Likewise, a corpus contrast or KL departure from a positional null is a descriptive diagnostic. Transformer-circuit and induction-head work elhage2021mathematical,olsson2022induction, and activation-patching methods meng2022locating,heimersheim2024how, motivate additional causal tests; a sign reversal alone does not identify their circuits.

Entropy and physical analogies.

Attention entropy, frequency-domain diagnostics and attention scaling are studied under different definitions and limits emnlp2025entropy,dope2025,criticalattn2025. Statistical-mechanical approaches to weights, training, generation or attention paths provide related but distinct objects soc2026,phasetransform2025,phasetransformsmall2025,cui2024phasetransition,nakaishi2024critical,attndissect2024,kim2026thermodynamic. Our \(Z_N\) is a finite sum; its infinite-support limit is \(\zeta (\gamma )\) only for \(\gamma {\gt}1\). The family inverse-temperature coordinate is not the model’s output sampling temperature.

The finite Shannon bound \(S_N\le \log N\) does not identify an entanglement entropy or establish a geometric area law for trained attention. Ryu–Takayanagi theory and work on learning its inverse mapping ryu2006holographic,jhep2026rttransformer do not validate that inference. No claim of being the first derivation from positional geometry is supported by the corrected argument. Historical comparisons and their original wording remain in the separate predecessor archive indexed by Appendix J.

Evidence at a glance

The initial predictor comparison has 18 model/corpus entries, of which 13 have a recorded base. On those 13, the mean absolute exponent error is \(0.167766\), and the median absolute relative error is \(19.2144\% \). The selected-case accuracy claim is withdrawn for the provenance reasons in Section 5.4. The separate October replay has 25 observations among 42 historical identifiers, including 17 unavailable observations. Only four successful job records identify an immutable weight revision. The historical text estimate lies inside the October interval in one of 25 comparisons; the stored Padé candidate and the October QL exponent have Spearman correlation \(-0.445\) on 19 available pairs. Differences in protocol prevent attributing these discrepancies to one cause.

On finite support, maximum entropy selects a unique power-law distribution at an interior prescribed log-distance moment. Entropy, Fisher information and formal heat capacity are computed by finite sums. They remain finite at \(\gamma =1\); the infinite-support summability boundary is not a demonstrated transition in finite-network capability. At \(N=2000\) and \(\gamma =1\), the discrete variance is \(5.48412\), compared with \(4.81448\) for the continuous density.

The November campaign records 8,064 interventions on 32 shared prompts for three models, including 1,152 zero-strength controls. Its improvements concern prediction of intervention effects, not improved model performance. Historical KV, retrieval, alignment and band-ablation experiments remain in their original sections with their protocol limitations.

How to use the results

Measure a profile under a declared protocol, compare alternative fitted families, and propagate its uncertainty into derived quantities. Test any proposed cache or rotary intervention against task and resource baselines. The manuscript establishes neither a configuration-only safe compression ratio nor a general context-extension or architecture-classification rule. Measurement time depends on model size, hardware and protocol; a universal three-minute CPU estimate is not supported.

3 \(\gamma \) as a Candidate Control Coordinate

3.1 From an observable to an intervention hypothesis

A fitted exponent describes an attention-distance profile under a specified corpus, support and aggregation. It does not determine the entire computation of a trained network. Within the finite family, for a statistic \(u\) independent of \(\gamma \), differentiation gives

\begin{equation} \partial _\gamma \mathbb E_{p_\gamma }[u] =-\operatorname {Cov}_{p_\gamma }(u,\log d). \tag {3} \end{equation}
3

For increasing \(u(d)\), this derivative is nonpositive: increasing the positive family exponent shifts mass toward shorter distances. This statement does not identify a model intervention that realises a chosen change in \(\gamma \). The former task bands at \(0.65\) and \(0.85\) have no established universal decision status. Their original interpretation is preserved in the separate predecessor archive, not used as a deployment classification here.

3.2 Three levers with different mechanisms

Choosing a frequency schedule before training, changing rotary frequencies at inference, and modifying individual attention heads are different interventions. They require separate controls. Attention-score temperature is also distinct from output sampling temperature. A covariance identity for the chosen family cannot predict the full response of learned queries, keys and downstream states. The per-head profiles in Section 14.3 motivate measurement at finer resolution, while their missing layers limit whole-model conclusions.

For the candidate alone,

\[ \partial _\theta \gamma _P= \frac{4T\sqrt2}{(2\theta +T\sqrt2)^2}{\gt}0. \]

Thus increasing \(\theta \) increases the candidate exponent at fixed \(T\). This corrects the direction of the earlier proposed controller; it does not prove that a trained model follows this derivative.

3.3 Candidate curves and historical observations

3.4 A measurement and evaluation workflow

  1. Define the task, evaluation context and baseline resource budget.

  2. Record model, tokenizer and corpus revisions, attention backend, precision, query selection, support and estimator; estimate profile uncertainty.

  3. Compute any family quantities on the stated support. Treat inverse Padé as a proposed experimental setting, not a task-optimal prescription.

  4. Evaluate interventions on held-out sequences with paired baselines, recording both task quality and actual memory or latency changes.

The thermostat in Section 12.3 remains an unvalidated controller proposal. A measured response and a stability analysis are necessary before any runtime control claim.

4 Background and Notation

We distinguish the rotary map, a count of completed cycles, and distances derived from that count. None of these definitions alone determines the learned attention distribution.

4.1 Rotary Position Encoding

Let \(h=d_{\rm head}\) be the query/key head dimension and let \(d_{\rm rot}=2m\le h\), \(m\ge 1\), be the actual rotary dimension. Standard geometric RoPE su2024roformer rotates \(m\) two-dimensional planes. For \(\theta {\gt}1\) and zero-based plane index \(i\),

\begin{equation} \omega _i=\theta ^{-i/m},\qquad i=0,\ldots ,m-1.\tag {4}\end{equation}
4

The frequencies range from \(1\) to \(\theta ^{-(m-1)/m}\). The slowest period is exactly \(2\pi \theta ^{(m-1)/m}\), approaching \(2\pi \theta \) only as \(m\to \infty \). Partial RoPE leaves \(h-2m\) coordinates unrotated; altered frequency schedules require their actual frequencies rather than this geometric formula.

For fixed content vectors \(q,k\) and rotations \(R\), orthogonality gives \((R(m_0)q)^\top R(n_0)k=q^\top R(n_0-m_0)k\). The explicit positional factor depends on the signed relative displacement. It need not be even in that displacement because the full score has a sine term. Content vectors can themselves depend on the surrounding context, so this identity does not imply that attention depends only on absolute distance or guarantee positional generalization.

Clock analogy. A plane records a phase modulo \(2\pi \) at every distance, including before its first full turn. Completing one turn is a threshold event in the unwrapped phase; it does not make the plane constant or erase all information in the joint vector of phases. Different clock readings can distinguish ideal positions, but usable discrimination also depends on weights, precision and noise.

4.2 Completed Cycles and the Uncycled-Plane Count

Definition 4.1 Cycled and uncycled planes
#
📕 p. 15📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

For real distance \(d{\gt}0\), call plane \(i\) cycled when \(d\omega _i\ge 2\pi \). The legacy symbols \(n_\mathrm {dead}\) and \(n_\mathrm {active}\) denote cycled and uncycled counts, respectively; they do not classify functional usefulness.

\begin{equation} n_\mathrm {dead}(d)=\min \left\{ m,\max \left\{ 0,1+\left\lfloor m\frac{\log (d/2\pi )}{\log \theta }\right\rfloor \right\} \right\} . \end{equation}
5

\begin{equation} n_\mathrm {active}(d)=m-n_\mathrm {dead}(d).\end{equation}
6

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

Proof ▼

Since \(\log \theta {\gt}0\), the threshold is equivalent to \(i\le x=m\log (d/2\pi )/\log \theta \). Among integers \(0,\ldots ,m-1\), the number satisfying this inequality is zero for \(x{\lt}0\), \(1+\lfloor x\rfloor \) for \(0\le x{\lt}m-1\), and \(m\) for \(x\ge m-1\). Clipping combines these cases and includes equality at the threshold. Subtracting from \(m\) gives the uncycled count.

💡 In plain words

The count separates the planes that have completed at least one turn from those that have not yet completed one at a given distance. The threshold is computed with the actual rotary frequencies and clipped between zero and \(m\).

Scope.

Completing a turn does not mean losing information or ceasing to attend. The Figure 2 lab checks the exact count against the continuous approximation.

🧪 Lab: Figure 2 live: turn the rotary-cycle surface in 3D

Turn the exact uncycled-fraction surface over log distance and log RoPE base. The star marks your values; the flat curve below compares the integer count with its clipped continuous approximation. This counts geometric phase thresholds, not attention decay.

A convenient continuous approximation is

\[ \widetilde n_{\rm active}(d)=m\left[1-\frac{\log (d/2\pi )}{\log \theta }\right]_0^1, \qquad [u]_0^1=\min (1,\max (0,u)). \]

Its absolute error is at most one plane. For the fraction, the error is at most \(1/m\); relative error against a small or zero exact count has no uniform bound. The staircase and the clipped straight line are bookkeeping of phases, not a derivation of a power-law attention score. In particular, cycling does not imply that a coordinate contributes noise.

4.3 Three Reference Scales and the Exact Last-Cycle Distance

It is useful to retain three distinct reference scales, while separating their definitions. Only the first and third arise from the continuous count; the second is a chosen comparison coordinate.

Definition 4.2 Reference distances
#
📕 p. 17📍 map❝ cite⚠ report
\begin{align} T_\mathrm {cross}& =2\pi \sqrt\theta & & \text{(continuous half-count)}\\ d_\mathrm {alias}& =\theta /\sqrt2 & & \text{(comparison scale)}\\ T_{\rm max}& =2\pi \theta & & \text{(continuous zero-count)} \end{align}

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

💡 In plain words

The three distances are distinct reference coordinates. \(2\pi \sqrt\theta \) and \(2\pi \theta \) come from the continuous count; \(\theta /\sqrt2\) is a chosen comparison scale. For finite \(m\), the last turn occurs before \(2\pi \theta \).

Scope.

None of these distances by itself constitutes a limit on retrieval, on useful context or on KV compression.

For integer \(1\le r{\lt}m\), exactly \(r\) planes are cycled on

\[ 2\pi \theta ^{(r-1)/m}\le d{\lt}2\pi \theta ^{r/m}. \]

For even \(m\), take \(r=m/2\) to obtain the exact half-count interval. At its upper endpoint \(2\pi \sqrt\theta \), one additional plane cycles. The final plane cycles at \(T_{\rm last}=2\pi \theta ^{(m-1)/m}\), before \(T_{\rm max}\). Thus neither endpoint is a proof that position becomes undetectable. Also, \(\theta /\sqrt2\) is not the zero of the Padé exponent in this paper: that candidate vanishes at \(T=\sqrt2\theta \).

5 Modelling \(\gamma \): Geometry, Approximations and Empirical Tests

The rotary count is exact under its stated frequency schedule. A prediction for a trained attention exponent requires additional assumptions about content scores, normalization and aggregation. We develop the candidate construction explicitly, identify where those assumptions enter, and compare the result with saved measurements. The empirical fits do not prove the construction that motivated them.

5.1 The Empirical Starting Point

A power-law regression represents a sampled profile by

\begin{equation} \log A(d)=\log A_0-\widehat\gamma \log d+\epsilon _d.\tag {10}\end{equation}
10

Here \(A(d)\) is a protocol-specific aggregate and \(\epsilon _d\) is its fitted log residual. The E4 program averages finite attention entries across heads and layers at the last query position, then across prompts and seeds. It discards non-finite entries without recording their final fraction. Random tokens change the content distribution; they do not remove learned content interactions or instrumental confounds. The October QL procedure instead has its own fixed-context profile and bootstrap protocol (Section 8).

The E4 panel contains both good and poor fits: for example, Pythia-1.4B text has \(R^2=.841258\), while Pythia-2.8B text has \(R^2=.999287\) on only three distances. Thus there is no supported statement that every tested model has \(R^2{\gt}.95\), or that every curve spans 10–2000. A descriptive power-law fit is not an exact law and does not uniquely identify its generative mechanism.

Five representative saved E4 profiles. Points are the means on each record’s declared fitting grid; lines use both slope and intercept from that regression. Pythia-2.8B covers only 30–100. The legend reports each actual \(R^2\); no uniform fit-quality claim is imposed.

5.2 From Rotary Coordinates to a Candidate Score

Groups 7–8 in Appendix K provide the verified score-to-softmax bound and the cosine-integral remainder under explicit row-level hypotheses.

Step 1: exact score decomposition.

Let \(\delta =n-m_0\) be the signed key-minus-query displacement, let \(h\) be the full head dimension, and let \(J=R'(0)\). For the \(m=d_{\rm rot}/2\) rotated pairs and the unrotated remainder \(q_\perp ,k_\perp \), the ordinary scaled dot-product score is

\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} s(m_0,n)=\frac1{\sqrt h}\biggl\{ q_\perp ^\top k_\perp + \sum _{i=0}^{m-1}\bigl[& (q_i^\top k_i)\cos (\delta \omega _i)\\ & +(q_i^\top Jk_i)\sin (\delta \omega _i)\bigr]\biggr\} . \end{aligned}\tag {11}\end{equation}
11

This follows by expanding \(R(\delta \omega _i)=I\cos (\delta \omega _i)+J\sin (\delta \omega _i)\) in each plane. Additional attention biases and masks must be added separately. In split-half implementations the physical coordinate pairing must match the implementation before applying this identity to weight rows.

Step 2: a conditional score model.

A cosine can already be negative before a full cycle: at phase \(\pi \) it equals \(-1\). Conversely, completing a cycle does not make its contribution average to zero over content. Small query/key covariance does not establish either assertion. An explicit modelling hypothesis would be

\begin{equation} \mathbb E[s(d)]\approx b_0+a\, \widetilde n_{\rm active}(d).\tag {12}\end{equation}
12

The coefficient \(a\) carries the amplitudes and score scaling; setting it to one is an additional choice. On the unclipped part of the continuous count this ansatz has a logarithmic distance term with coefficient \(-am/\log \theta \) and intercept \(b_1=b_0+am(1+\log (2\pi )/\log \theta )\).

Step 3: a conditional normalization model.

If an idealized row has deterministic scores \(b_1-\kappa \log d\) on a fixed support, then its softmax is exactly a power law:

\begin{equation} p(d)=\frac{e^{b_1-\kappa \log d}}{\sum _{u=1}^{N}e^{b_1-\kappa \log u}}=\frac{d^{-\kappa }}{\sum _{u=1}^{N}u^{-\kappa }},\qquad \kappa =\frac{am}{\log \theta }.\tag {13}\end{equation}
13

Replacing random scores by their mean before softmax is not an identity. For equiprobable score vectors \((2,0)\) and \((0,0)\), the expected first softmax component is \(0.690399\), whereas the softmax of the mean gives \(0.731059\). Averaging across heads, query positions or contexts adds further noncommuting operations. In E4 the context length also changes with \(d\), so the normalization need not be the same across the plotted curve.

Pythia-70M has head dimension 64 but rotary dimension 16: its \(\texttt{rotary\_ pct}=0.25\) leaves only \(m=8\) rotated pairs. With \(a=1\) and \(\theta =10^4\), the conditional exponent is \(0.868589\), not \(3.474356\). Relative to the E4 text estimate \(0.747602\), the discrepancy is \(16.18\% \); the matched E4 uniform null is \(0.782582\). Correcting the dimension therefore does not validate the ansatz or its averaging assumptions. More directly, setting all query projections to zero gives uniform attention over unmasked keys for every RoPE base, provided no additional key-dependent score bias is present. That counterexample shows why RoPE geometry alone cannot force a nonzero power-law exponent.

A configuration check against fixed-query profiles.

Table 6 evaluates only the stipulated \(a=1\) ansatz, using \(m=d_{\rm rot}/2\) from saved configurations. The QL entries are the existing October text fits at \(T=2048\) in FP32. Every candidate lies outside its corresponding saved bootstrap interval. In particular, the two smallest rotary subspaces have the largest QL slopes in this six-row set; the slopes do not increase monotonically with \(m\) as this fixed-\(a\) candidate does. This is a descriptive negative check of that specification, not a controlled intervention on rotary dimension or a rejection of every learned score model. The score ansatz and the following rational candidate are different constructions. With a fixed alignment coefficient, \(\kappa =am/\log \theta \) depends on the rotary-pair count and has no context parameter; \(\gamma _P(\theta ,T)\) depends on context and omits that count. No identified relation between \(a,m,T\) connects them. The rational expression is a chosen configuration function, not a consequence of Steps 2–3.

A conditional cosine-integral alternative.

Writing \(S_m(d)=\sum _{i=0}^{m-1}\cos (d\theta ^{-i/m})\), its left Riemann approximation at fixed \(d,\theta {\gt}1\) is

\[ S_m(d)\approx \frac{m}{\log \theta }\int _{1/\theta }^1 \frac{\cos (d\omega )}{\omega }\, \mathrm d\omega =\frac{m}{\log \theta }[\operatorname {Ci}(d)-\operatorname {Ci}(d/\theta )]. \]

For \(1\ll d\ll \theta \), the bracket is \(\log \theta -\gamma _E-\log d+O(d^{-1}+(d/\theta )^2)\). These are two distinct approximations. The absolute Riemann-sum error is bounded by the total variation, hence by \(d(1-1/\theta )\); this bound need not be small for a finite rotary subspace. The normalized error tends to zero as \(m\to \infty \) at fixed \(d,\theta \), not uniformly over arbitrary growing distance ranges. On 400 geometrically spaced distances from 10 to 2000, \(m=32\), \(\theta =10^4\), the fitted sum slope is \(-3.480436\) versus \(-m/\log \theta =-3.474356\), while the largest pointwise error against the integral is \(6.868580\). Agreement of fitted slopes alone does not control the individual oscillations.

If pre-RoPE plane dot products have a common, distance-independent mean \(a\), sine contributions have zero mean, and other score components have constant mean, the mean-score slope is conditionally \(-am/(\sqrt{d_{\rm head}}\log \theta )\). Here \(a\) is an unscaled plane dot product, unlike the score-scaled coefficient in Step 2. Measuring these amplitudes and the pre-softmax slope with fixed queries is a test of the assumptions. It does not commute expectation with softmax or derive the rational candidate.

Dimensionless candidate.

Define \(z=T\sqrt2/\theta \), using a chosen context parameter \(T{\gt}0\). The linear candidate is

\begin{equation} \gamma _{\rm linear}=1-z=1-T\sqrt2/\theta .\tag {14}\end{equation}
14

The factor \(\sqrt2\) is part of this parametrization. It is not derived by the cycle count or by an asserted zero of a cosine sum at \(\theta /\sqrt2\). The actual half-count scale is discussed in Section 4.3. A negative exponent is mathematically admissible on finite support; whether it fits a particular observation is a separate question.

Proposition 5.1 Obstruction to the proposed cosine-sum inference
#
📕 p. 21📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

A finite cosine sum of the form

\begin{equation} S_K(d)=\frac1m\sum _{i=0}^{K-1}\cos (d\omega _i),\qquad 1\le K\le m,\end{equation}
15

is not automatically a nonnegative normalized attention distribution. In particular, the proposed ratio of logarithms cannot supply the Padé exponent:

\begin{equation} \frac{\log r}{\log (1/r)}=-1\ne \frac{2-z}{2+z},\quad r{\gt}0,\ r\ne 1,\ z{\gt}0.\end{equation}
16

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

Proof ▼

For \(r{\gt}0\), \(\log (1/r)=-\log r\), and \(r\ne 1\) makes the denominator nonzero. Also \((2-z)/(2+z){\gt}-1\) for \(z{\gt}0\). A one-term cosine sum is negative when its phase is \(\pi \). These observations block the stated normalization and exponent inference. A stationary-phase argument would require an explicit asymptotic parameter, amplitude hypotheses and a controlled remainder; none is supplied by the finite sum alone.

💡 In plain words

A finite sum of cosines can be negative and does not by itself define an attention distribution. Moreover, the proposed ratio of logarithms equals exactly \(-1\) on its domain, whereas the Padé candidate is greater than \(-1\) for \(z{\gt}0\). The proposition blocks that derivation; it does not rule out that another hypothesis on scores could produce a power law.

Formal scope.

The paper gives a direct algebraic proof. This full statement has no Isabelle link in this Blueprint.

5.3 The Padé Candidate and Its Domain

The rational candidate

\begin{equation} \gamma _P(\theta ,T)=\frac{2\theta -T\sqrt2}{2\theta +T\sqrt2}=\frac{2-z}{2+z},\qquad z=\frac{T\sqrt2}{\theta },\tag {17}\end{equation}
17

is the \([1,1]\) Padé approximant to \(e^{-z}\) at zero, since both have expansion \(1-z+z^2/2+O(z^3)\). This local approximation theorem does not identify an observed exponent with \(e^{-z}\). For \(z{\gt}0\), \(-1{\lt}\gamma _P{\lt}1\); it is positive only for \(z{\lt}2\), vanishes at \(T=\sqrt2\theta \), and approaches \(-1\) as \(z\to \infty \). It therefore cannot predict observed exponents above one. Its derivatives describe the candidate function, not the response of trained weights to an intervention.

Approximation comparison.

The following are distinct candidate formulas, not successive increasing orders of one validated attention expansion:

\begin{equation} 1,\qquad 1-z,\qquad e^{-z},\qquad \frac{2-z}{2+z},\qquad \frac1{1+z}.\tag {18}\end{equation}
18

The last function is \([0,1]\), with expansion \(1-z+z^2+O(z^3)\); it is not a higher-order approximation than \([1,1]\). For \(z{\gt}0\), its excess over \(\gamma _P\) is \(z^2/[(1+z)(2+z)]{\gt}0\). Selecting it after observing that an exponent exceeds \(\gamma _P\) uses the target to choose the predictor and does not establish prospective accuracy. Neither SWA nor GQA implies this correction. A context-window hypothesis must use the actual masking schedule and head/layer aggregation.

Implementation hypothesis.

A rational expression may be inexpensive to evaluate, but no gate is proved near-optimal by that fact. Routing quality, normalization, sparse-kernel cost and task error require direct benchmarking. The exponent parameter \(z=T\sqrt2/\theta \) must not silently become a per-distance kernel argument.

An algebraic shifted-base coordinate is

\begin{equation} \theta _{\rm eff}=\theta +T/\sqrt2.\tag {19}\end{equation}
19

It gives the identity \(\gamma _P=1-T\sqrt2/\theta _{\rm eff}\) for this definition. It is not the base producing the same exponent at \(T=0\), since every positive base gives \(\gamma _P=1\) there. Nor is it the inverse fitted-base coordinate in Section 9; those are different definitions and cannot jointly diagnose training history.

Unreconstructed selected-case statistic.

The earlier \(4.3\% \) median was attributed to nine selected “non-anomalous” cases. Neither an unambiguous nine-row membership list nor the selection and denominator calculation was recovered. The surviving Padé comparison JSON contains five entries and uses a prediction denominator; it does not establish the claimed nine-case statistic. We therefore withdraw that number as an accuracy result, rather than choose nine rows after observing their errors. The 13 identifiable comparisons here remain available in full, with the observed-exponent denominator stated above.

🖼️ Figure 6

All 13 computable residuals, without excluding poorly predicted observations. Lack of fit is a limitation of the candidate; the residual alone does not identify its cause.

Across these 13 entries, mean absolute error is \(0.167766\), median absolute error \(0.124555\), and median absolute relative error \(19.2144\% \), using \(|\widehat\gamma |\) in the denominator. These are descriptive errors on a mixed initial panel, not an out-of-sample benchmark. The earlier selected-case percentages do not transfer to this denominator. In the separate October replay, only one historical text exponent lies in its corresponding interval among 25 observations, and the stored Padé comparison has rank correlation \(-0.445\) on 19 rows (Section 8).

Trivial predictors on the same 13 rows.

The mean absolute errors are \(0.182656\) for the constant one, \(0.177669\) for the panel mean and \(0.172106\) for the panel median, compared with \(0.167766\) for \(\gamma _P\). The latter improves on the median by only \(0.004340\) (about \(2.52\% \)). The mean and median use this same panel, so this is an in-sample descriptive comparison, not a held-out baseline experiment or proof of zero predictive information. Prospective usefulness has not been demonstrated. Adding present-day public bases to the five missing fields would be a separate imputation analysis; it would not recover the configurations of those historical executions.

5.5 Exploratory Five-Axis Regression

The original exploratory specification regresses the text exponent on five covariates:

\begin{equation} \widehat\gamma _t=\beta _0+\beta _P\gamma _P+\beta _c(\widehat\gamma _t-\widehat\gamma _r)+\beta _G\mathbf1_{\rm GQA}+\beta _S\mathbf1_{\rm SWA}+\beta _{\rm IH}\mathbf1_{\rm post-IH}+\varepsilon .\tag {20}\end{equation}
20

The source script supplies manual architecture flags, a \(T=100\) candidate parameter, and a size-derived “post-IH” flag; the latter is not a measured circuit label. Replaying its 23-row design matrix reproduces the following coefficients. This is a check of the original regression specification, not an endorsement of its metadata or identification assumptions.

The fit has \(R^2=0.437821\), adjusted \(R^2=0.272474\), and residual standard deviation \(0.164644\). The corpus covariate contains the response \(\widehat\gamma _t\) itself, so the regression is not a configuration-only predictor and its apparent explanatory power can include target leakage. The near-constant Padé column is also nearly collinear with the intercept. A ratio of predictor variance to observed variance is not variance explained; unexplained variance cannot automatically be assigned to the other axes.

The largest original-specification residuals are approximately \(+.47\) (Pythia-31M), \(-.33\) (SmolLM2-135M), \(-.26\) (OLMo-7B), \(-.19\) (Pythia-2.8B) and \(-.18\) (Llama-2-7B). They motivate tests of tokenization, data, optimization and measurement support but do not identify these factors. In particular, the unequal-support Pythia-2.8B corpus contrast needs the correction in Section 8.4.

A useful hypothesis notation remains

\begin{equation} \gamma _{\rm obs}=\gamma _P+\delta _{\rm data}+\delta _{\rm arch}+\delta _{\rm circuit}+\delta _{\rm train}+\varepsilon .\tag {21}\end{equation}
21

Without interventions or identifying restrictions, infinitely many assignments of the \(\delta \) terms give the same residual. The decomposition does not establish a geometric ceiling, a fixed median, or that the perturbations explain \(99\% \) of variance. Measured exponents above one already exceed the positive-\(z\) range of \(\gamma _P\).

5.6 Derived Quantities and Testable Consequences

P1: entropy conditional on the family.

For the finite family, the identity is

\begin{equation} H_\gamma (N)=\log Z_N+\gamma U_N,\qquad U_N=-\partial _\gamma \log Z_N.\tag {22}\end{equation}
22

The entropy columns in the initial thermodynamic dataset were derived from fitted exponents; they are not independent entropy observations. A test must instead measure a normalized empirical distribution on the same support and compare its entropy with the fitted-family value, accounting for estimation uncertainty. Normalizing values at seven sampled distances gives the entropy of a seven-point variable, which cannot be directly equated with entropy over 2000 token distances.

P2: entropy-based effective count.

The exponential of Shannon entropy is

\begin{equation} L_{\rm eff}:=N_{\rm eff}:=e^{H_\gamma (N)}=\prod _{d=1}^{N}p_\gamma (d)^{-p_\gamma (d)}=Z_N\prod _{d=1}^{N}d^{\gamma p_\gamma (d)}.\tag {23}\end{equation}
23

The product uses probability weights \(p_\gamma (d)\), not uniform weights \(1/N\). For \(N=2000\), exact finite sums give \(N_{\rm eff}=1160.379\) at \(\gamma =.65\) and \(362.107\) at \(.95\). For fixed \(0{\lt}\gamma {\lt}1\), \(N_{\rm eff}/N\to e^{-\gamma /(1-\gamma )}/(1-\gamma )\); for fixed \(\gamma {\gt}1\), \(N_{\rm eff}\) tends to a finite constant and \(N_{\rm eff}/N\to 0\). These are diversity measures of the chosen distance distribution. They do not bound multi-hop reasoning spans, factuality or the number of useful tokens in a trained network.

P3: layer variation with missing fits reported.

We recompute layer means from finite entries of the saved per-head exponent matrices, exclude the actual first and last architecture layers, and report the population standard deviation across the remaining observed layer means. Entirely missing interior layers remain missing; they are not reclassified as boundary layers. Some observed layers also lack individual head fits, as recorded in the evidence manifest.

Four of five available-case summaries have \(\mathrm{CV}{\lt}.20\), and only one has \(\mathrm{CV}{\lt}.15\). Pythia-1.4B has \(\mathrm{CV}=.257442\). The data do not establish a universal layer-stability bound or a geometric cause. In particular, partial matrices cannot certify whole-model stability. The former procedure removed the last observed layer after filtering missing layers, which need not remove the architectural boundary.

P4: short- and long-distance residuals.

Flattening at short distance and faster decay at long distance are testable candidate patterns. They are not consequences of “all planes uncycled below \(2\pi \sqrt\theta \)”, which is false: the first threshold is \(2\pi \). Training length also does not force every phase to alias uniformly. The saved BLOOM-1b7 extended-distance record contains a numerical zero at \(d=5000\), with non-monotonic positive values at 2048 and 3000. A numerical zero in one ALiBi experiment is not a theorem about RoPE or proof of a universal hard cutoff. Testing residual signs requires a predeclared fitting interval, actual training context and adequate positive observations in each region.

Null baselines on the available saved fits.

We compare power-law and exponential regressions in log-attention space on each record’s declared distance grid, using canonical text/random files with at least three positive points and a stored fit. The resulting set has 74 profiles, of which 72 favor the power law by in-sample \(R^2\); the median difference is \(+.203803\). The manifest lists every included record. This is a descriptive model-form comparison, with unequal ranges and no held-out evaluation. It does not rule out mixtures, content-dependent mechanisms, or learned-only explanations, and it does not prove a MaxEnt constraint. Correlation across architectures cannot exclude training or data as a cause.

6 Why Power Law: The Maximum Entropy Foundation

The finite power-law family follows from a specified entropy-maximization problem. The constraint and the reference measure are premises of that problem. RoPE’s frequency geometry does not establish that a trained attention distribution solves it. This section supplies the conditional mathematical result and its connection to measured profiles.

Theorem 6.1 MaxEnt selection at a prescribed family moment

📕 p. 27📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

Let \(N\ge 1\) be an integer and \(\gamma \in \mathbb R\). Define

\[ p_\gamma (d)=\frac{d^{-\gamma }}{Z_N(\gamma )},\qquad Z_N(\gamma )=\sum _{j=1}^N j^{-\gamma },\qquad d\in \{ 1,\ldots ,N\} . \]

Among all probability vectors \(p\) on this support satisfying \(\mathbb E_p[\log d]=\mathbb E_{p_\gamma }[\log d]\), the unique entropy maximizer is \(p_\gamma \). We use counting measure, natural logarithms and \(0\log 0=0\).

Lean · ours, in partshow

Lean proves the Gibbs inequality and equality for the finite family; the paper statement allows any real exponent and N=1, while the linked Lean file treats N>0 and the existence result is stated for a positive exponent.

🆕 Classical and new: Classical maximum-entropy result with a prescribed constraint; it does not prove a training law.

↳ Used in: Theorem 6.2

Proof ▼

The reference vector is strictly positive. Since \(\log p_\gamma (d)=-\gamma \log d-\log Z_N\), the moment and normalization constraints give \(\sum p\log p_\gamma =\sum p_\gamma \log p_\gamma \). Consequently,

\[ H(p_\gamma )-H(p) =\sum _{d=1}^N p(d)\log \frac{p(d)}{p_\gamma (d)}\ge 0. \]

Gibbs’ inequality applies also when some entries of \(p\) vanish. Equality holds only for \(p=p_\gamma \). This proves global optimality and uniqueness, rather than only a stationary point of a Lagrangian.

💡 In plain words

On a finite support, if the mean of \(\log d\) is fixed at the value of a given power family, that family uniquely maximizes the entropy. The proof compares entropies through the KL divergence and uses its non-negativity. The fixed moment is a mathematical premise, not a consequence of RoPE or of training a model.

Formal scope.

The argument is written in the paper. Lean verifies the Gibbs inequality for the finite family; the full statement for every exponent and \(N=1\) keeps a written proof here, with no formal certificate of the same scope.

[colback=ModernTint,colframe=ModernTeal,title=What the constraint does and does not select,fontupper=] Exponential, Gaussian-shaped or cutoff distributions on a finite set can have the same log-distance moment. They are not excluded as empirical models of attention. The theorem singles out the entropy maximizer among feasible distributions. Competing profile families must be compared on the same observations, support and loss; differentiability in distance is not required on a discrete support.

Example: a six-sided die. If the only prescribed statistic is the average of \(\log (\mathrm{face})\), choosing maximum entropy assigns \(p(k)\propto k^{-\gamma }\) on \(\{ 1,\ldots ,6\} \). This is an inference rule under limited information. It does not establish that a physical loaded die, or a trained transformer, must realize that rule.

For integer \(N{\gt}1\) and \(0{\lt}\lambda {\lt}\log N\), consider

\begin{align} & \max _{p\ge 0}\ H(p)=-\sum _{d=1}^N p(d)\log p(d),\\ & \sum _{d=1}^N p(d)=1,\qquad \sum _{d=1}^N p(d)\log d=\lambda . \end{align}

There is a unique real exponent and a unique maximizing distribution:

\begin{equation} p^*(d)=\frac{d^{-\gamma }}{Z_N(\gamma )},\qquad -\partial _\gamma \log Z_N(\gamma )=\lambda . \end{equation}
26

The exponent is positive, zero or negative according as \(\lambda \) is below, equal to or above \(\log (N!)/N\). At the endpoints \(\lambda =0\) and \(\lambda =\log N\), the feasible distribution is the point mass at \(1\) or \(N\), respectively, obtained as an exponent limit. For \(N=1\) the distribution is unique but the exponent is unidentifiable.

🆕 Classical and new: Explicit application of Gibbs and of the strict ordering of the moment; a conditional mathematical result.

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

Proof ▼

The Lagrangian \(\mathcal L=H(p)-\mu (\sum p-1)-\gamma (\sum p\log d-\lambda )\) has stationary equation \(-\log p(d)-1-\mu -\gamma \log d=0\). Normalization gives the displayed family. To establish existence of the required exponent, define \(U_N(\gamma )=\mathbb E_{p_\gamma }[\log d]\). Finite-sum differentiation gives

\[ U_N'(\gamma )=-\operatorname {Var}_{p_\gamma }(\log d){\lt}0, \qquad U_N(0)=\frac{\log (N!)}{N}. \]

Strict negativity follows because all probabilities are positive and \(\log d\) is nonconstant for \(N{\gt}1\). As \(\gamma \to +\infty \), mass concentrates at \(1\) and \(U_N\to 0\); as \(\gamma \to -\infty \), it concentrates at \(N\) and \(U_N\to \log N\). Continuity and strict monotonicity establish existence, uniqueness and the sign condition. The preceding Gibbs argument then proves global optimality over all feasible vectors, including their boundary.

💡 In plain words

For an interior log-distance moment, there is exactly one exponent of the finite family that attains it. The derivative of the moment is minus a strictly positive variance, which gives the ordering and uniqueness; the Gibbs argument of the preceding theorem gives global optimality. The endpoints require limits of exponents and, if \(N=1\), the exponent cannot be identified.

Formal scope.

Lean verifies existence, uniqueness and optimality for the interior moment that gives a positive exponent. The zero- or negative-exponent regimes and the endpoints of the full statement remain proved in the manuscript.

Interpretation

The theorem is a constrained inference result, not a training-dynamics result. Its premise must be justified separately when the family is applied to attention. Models with identical RoPE configuration can learn different queries and keys and produce different profiles. The exploratory five-axis panel in Section 5.5 reports a population residual standard deviation \(0.164644\) (approximately \(0.16\)) in its exploratory multiple regression, not a measured variance at fixed configuration; neither that regression nor an assumed centroid turns the MaxEnt premise into a geometric necessity.

6.2 Thermodynamic Interpretation

The family can be written in Gibbs form:

\begin{equation} p_\gamma (d)=\frac{e^{-\gamma \log d}}{Z_N(\gamma )},\qquad H(d)=\log d,\qquad T_{\rm attn}=1/\gamma \quad (\gamma \ne 0). \tag {27} \end{equation}
27

This is a mathematical dictionary for a chosen probability family. The inverse-temperature coordinate is not the output sampling temperature, and the dictionary alone does not identify a physical equilibrium process or a trained model’s response to an intervention.

Quantity

Formula

Scope

Inverse temperature

\(\gamma \)

Family parameter, not a measured physical temperature.

Temperature

\(1/\gamma \)

Defined for \(\gamma \ne 0\); increasing positive \(\gamma \) favors shorter distances.

Partition function

\(\sum _{d=1}^N d^{-\gamma }\)

Finite for every finite \(N\); the infinite sum converges only for \(\gamma {\gt}1\).

Heat capacity

\(-\gamma ^2 U_N'(\gamma )\)

A finite-family susceptibility, not task sensitivity.

For \(S=\log Z_N+\gamma U_N\), differentiation cancels the two terms involving \(U_N\) alone. Since \(U_N'{\lt}0\) for \(N{\gt}1\), the parameterization gives

\[ \frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm d\gamma }=\gamma \frac{\mathrm dU_N}{\mathrm d\gamma }, \qquad \frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dU_N}=\gamma \quad (N{\gt}1). \]

6.3 Duality with Zipf’s Law

Zipf’s vocabulary law zipf1949human and a distance power law can both be represented by constrained-entropy families. For two members of the same finite power-law family with integer \(N{\gt}1\), strict monotonicity of its log moment identifies equal exponents. This requires the same support and reference measure and the family assumption:

\begin{equation} \mathbb E[\log \mathrm{rank}]=\mathbb E[\log d] \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \alpha =\gamma \quad \text{same family, support and measure; }N{\gt}1. \tag {28} \end{equation}
28

Vocabulary ranks and token distances generally have different supports. The seven successful saved pairs give \(r(\alpha _{\rm Zipf},\gamma )=-0.505314\). No corrected positive correlation is established. The three Pythia rows have constant rank exponent, so their within-group Pearson correlation is undefined (Appendix D).

6.4 Finite Thermodynamic Functions

Group 5 in Appendix K gives the full smoothness, entropy and divergence statements for this finite family, with proofs.

The discrete quantities are defined by exact sums: [nobreak=true]

\begin{align} Z_N(\gamma )& =\sum _{d=1}^N d^{-\gamma },\qquad Z_N(1)=H_N,\tag {29}\\ U_N(\gamma )& =\frac{\sum _{d=1}^N d^{-\gamma }\log d}{Z_N(\gamma )},\\ C_V(\gamma ,N)& =-\gamma ^2\partial _\gamma U_N =\gamma ^2\operatorname {Var}_{p_\gamma }(\log d). \end{align}

Separately, with Lebesgue measure on \([1,N]\), the continuous normalizer is

\[ Z_c(\gamma ,N)=\begin{cases} (N^{1-\gamma }-1)/(1-\gamma ),& \gamma \ne 1,\\ \log N,& \gamma =1. \end{cases} \]

The continuous and discrete moments must not be mixed. A tail fit on \([16,T/2]\) does not establish this family over all of \([1,N]\). The support and whether a quantity is measured or calculated from an exponent accompany each application.

Derived numerical examples

At \(N=2000\), using the full-precision replayed exponents of P10, P06, P13, P16 and P17, respectively, the family heat capacities are \(2.5396\), \(1.8335\), \(5.4488\), \(5.9361\) and \(6.5951\). These are the same inputs and rounding convention as Section 8. The discrete maximum is near \(\gamma =1.256885\), with \(C_V=6.919812\). These are calculations for the stipulated family, not moments measured from model attention rows.

7 Finite Power-Law Families and Infinite-Support Limits

7.1 The Partition Function and Phase Structure

For a fixed real exponent, the infinite-support limit of the discrete normalizer distinguishes three summability regimes:

\begin{align} \gamma {\lt}1:& \quad Z_N(\gamma )\sim N^{1-\gamma }/(1-\gamma )\to \infty ,\tag {32}\\ \gamma =1:& \quad Z_N(1)=H_N\sim \log N\to \infty ,\\ \gamma {\gt}1:& \quad Z_N(\gamma )\to \zeta (\gamma ){\lt}\infty . \end{align}

Every finite-\(N\) distribution remains normalized. Divergence of the unnormalized infinite sum means that the same weights cannot be normalized on all positive integers; it does not mean a model has infinite attention mass or unbounded retrieval ability. For \(\gamma {\gt}1\) the limiting distribution still has an infinite tail, not a hard finite horizon. The term Hagedorn hagedorn1965statistical denotes an analogy to a summability boundary, not an identification with a physical phase transition. Analogy and its limit. A change of regime can be pictured as a phase boundary. Unlike a boiling or freezing system, however, the finite sums here are analytic functions of \(\gamma \). The mathematical limit \(N\to \infty \) must be distinguished from an intervention on a finite-context network.

Proof ▼

Write \(L=\log N\). The change of variable \(y=\log x\), with \(\mathrm dy=\mathrm dx/x\), maps the density to the uniform distribution on \([0,L]\). Direct integration gives

\[ \mathbb E_{p_c}[\log x]=\frac{\log N}{2},\qquad \mathbb E_{p_c}[(\log x)^2]=\frac{(\log N)^2}{3}. \]

Subtracting the square of the first moment from the second gives \(L^2/3-L^2/4=L^2/12\). This calculation concerns the continuous density, not harmonic probabilities on integer distances.

💡 In plain words

For the continuous density \(1/(x\log N)\), the change of variables \(y=\log x\) gives a uniform distribution on \([0,\log N]\). Its variance is \((\log N)^2/12\). This continuous computation differs from the variance of the integer distances and does not establish a phase transition in a transformer.

Formal scope.

Lean verifies the algebraic identity of the two moments. The transformation of the density and the continuous integrals are proved in the manuscript.

Equivalent continuous expansion

For \(\epsilon =1-\gamma \) and fixed \(L\), \(Z_c=(e^{\epsilon L}-1)/\epsilon \) has a removable singularity at zero. Its analytic expansion gives

\[ \log Z_c=\log L+\frac{\epsilon L}{2} +\frac{\epsilon ^2L^2}{24}+O(\epsilon ^3),\qquad U_c=\frac L2+\frac{\epsilon L^2}{12}+O(\epsilon ^2). \]

Taking the derivative at \(\epsilon =0\) recovers the same variance. The remainder terms are essential: a truncated expansion is not an exact expression for \(U_c\) away from one, and a first-order normalizer is insufficient for its second derivative.

For discrete token distances, the exact value instead is

\[ C_V(1,N)=\frac{\sum _{d=1}^N(\log d)^2/d}{H_N} -\left(\frac{\sum _{d=1}^N\log d/d}{H_N}\right)^2. \]

At \(N=2000\), the continuous value is \(4.81448\), while the discrete value is \(5.48412\). Finite-sum calculation places the discrete maximum near \(\gamma =1.256885\), with \(C_V=6.919812\). Both remain finite. These numbers are derived family calculations, not independent measurements on language models.

7.3 Fisher Information and Heat Capacity

On fixed finite support, \(\partial _\gamma \log p_\gamma (d)=U_N-\log d\). Squaring and averaging therefore gives

\begin{equation} I(\gamma )=\mathbb E_{p_\gamma }[(\partial _\gamma \log p_\gamma )^2] =\operatorname {Var}_{p_\gamma }(\log d) =\partial _\gamma ^2\log Z_N(\gamma ). \tag {36} \end{equation}
38

\begin{equation} C_V(\gamma )=\gamma ^2 I(\gamma ),\qquad I(\gamma )=C_V(\gamma )/\gamma ^2\quad (\gamma \ne 0). \tag {37} \end{equation}
39

At \(\gamma =0\), \(I\) is evaluated directly as a variance; division by \(\gamma ^2\) is not defined. Neither quantity is singular at finite \(N\). Their extrema need not coincide because \(C_V'=2\gamma I+\gamma ^2 I'\). For \(N{\gt}1\), the intrinsic Fisher length inside this one-parameter family is

\begin{equation*} d_{\rm FR}(\gamma _1,\gamma _2)= \left|\int _{\gamma _1}^{\gamma _2}\sqrt{I(\gamma )}\, \mathrm d\gamma \right|. \end{equation*}

The integral uses \(\sqrt I\), not \(I\). This is a distance along the specified statistical family; it is not automatically the ambient simplex geodesic or a distance between trained networks with different protocols.

Proof ▼

The first part is the finite-alphabet Shannon bound, with equality only at the uniform vector. For \(N{\gt}1\), the power-law vector is uniform exactly when \(\gamma =0\). For the second part, integral comparison (or Euler–Maclaurin with fixed exponent) gives \(Z_N=N^{1-\gamma }/(1-\gamma )+O(1)\) and \(U_N=\log N-1/(1-\gamma )+O(N^{\gamma -1}\log N)\). Substitute into \(S=\log Z_N+\gamma U_N\). At one, \(H_N=\log N+\gamma _E+O(N^{-1})\) and \(\sum _{d\le N}\log d/d=\tfrac 12(\log N)^2+O(1)\) yield the stated separate expansion. Above one, both \(\sum d^{-\gamma }\) and \(\sum d^{-\gamma }\log d\) converge, giving the zeta expression. The fixed-exponent remainder bounds are not uniform as \(\gamma \to 1\).

💡 In plain words

The entropy of a distribution over \(N\) distances does not exceed \(\log N\). The power family moreover has three distinct asymptotic regimes: fixed exponent less than one, equal to one and greater than one. The formula of the first regime cannot be substituted directly at one because its remainder is not uniform as that point is approached.

Formal scope.

Lean verifies the finite bound and its uniform equality case; the three asymptotic expansions are proved in the manuscript. None of them is a measurement of models.

Calculated model-panel quantities

For the 21 initial-panel model/corpus entries in Section 8, exact finite-family entropies at \(N=2000\) range from \(4.377455\) to \(7.477491\). Each value is calculated from the corresponding replayed exponent, not independently measured from attention. Their association with \(\gamma \) cannot validate the finite-alphabet theorem or a physical mechanism. The table reports the input exponents and the derived values together.

Scope of the holographic analogy

The Ryu–Takayanagi relation ryu2006holographic concerns entanglement entropy and geometric areas in its stated physical setting. A logarithmic Shannon bound for a distance variable establishes neither that setting nor a central charge \(c=3\). Matching its leading coefficient to a CFT formula is insufficient. Likewise, the bound does not create thermodynamic pressure that reallocates rotary coordinates to semantic content. Such a channel interpretation requires separate functional evidence. Work on learning inverse holographic maps jhep2026rttransformer concerns a different learning problem and does not identify the operator or geometry of the models studied here.

Threshold-count exponent \(1/\gamma \)

For the normalized family, a probability threshold has the finite-support count

\[ \# \{ d\in \{ 1,\ldots ,N\} :p_\gamma (d)\ge \epsilon \} =\min \! \left\{ N,\left\lfloor (\epsilon Z_N)^{-1/\gamma }\right\rfloor \right\} , \qquad \gamma {\gt}0,\quad \epsilon {\gt}0. \]

\begin{equation} d_{\rm eff}:=1/\gamma \quad (\gamma {\gt}0). \tag {40} \end{equation}
41

The notation \(d_{\rm eff}\) records an exponent of threshold scaling, not a Hausdorff or box-counting dimension of model states. The unnormalized weights \(d^{-\gamma }\) give \(\lfloor \epsilon ^{-1/\gamma }\rfloor \) before clipping to \(N\). The examples \(\gamma =.674\) and \(1.045\) yield \(1/\gamma \approx 1.48\) and \(0.96\), respectively; at one the reciprocal is one. These arithmetic values do not prove a fractal support, measure-zero addressability or exclusion of hyperbolic architectures such as Hypformer chen2024hypformer. Measuring a geometric dimension of per-head support is a separate proposed experiment.

Band ablation measurements in EXP-B3

The full saved window sweep and exact mask audit are in Section 13, Table 24. The historical groups are unequal adjacent-coordinate masks rather than two sets of intact rotary planes. The larger mask has higher PPL at every saved window. Neither the finite entropy bound nor those ablations establish a semantic reservoir or a semantic/positional double dissociation. The schematic has been replaced by the recorded PPL curves in Figure 13.

7.5 The Family with an Exponential Cutoff

A second family adds a cutoff coefficient \(\lambda \ge 0\); here \(\lambda \) is distinct from the prescribed log moment in Section 6. Its infinite-support normalizer, when convergent, is

\begin{equation} Z_\infty (\gamma ,\lambda )=\operatorname {Li}_\gamma (e^{-\lambda }) =\sum _{d=1}^\infty d^{-\gamma }e^{-\lambda d}. \tag {41} \end{equation}
42

Definition 7.3 Summability regimes
#
📕 p. 33📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

At \(\lambda =0,\gamma =1\), \(Z_N=H_N\sim \log N\). The other cases are

\begin{align} \lambda =0,\ \gamma {\lt}1:& \quad Z_N\sim N^{1-\gamma }/(1-\gamma )\to \infty ,\\ \lambda =0,\ \gamma {\gt}1:& \quad Z_N\to \zeta (\gamma ){\lt}\infty ,\\ \lambda {\gt}0:& \quad Z_\infty {\lt}\infty \quad (\gamma \in \mathbb R). \end{align}

Cite: Definition 7.3, p. 33, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24379538

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

💡 In plain words

The definition classifies when the normalizer of a power family with a possible exponential cutoff on infinite support converges. With a positive cutoff it converges for every exponent; without a cutoff, the summability threshold is at one.

Scope.

These are cases of a mathematical distribution. They do not automatically classify architectures or prove a phase transition in trained models.

These are distributional cases, not an automatic partition of architectures. An ALiBi bias may motivate an exponential positional factor, but learned content scores also contribute. The reported mean distances of 19 tokens for BLOOM and 772 for Falcon remain panel observations; they are not implied by the normalizer alone.

Exploratory size regression

The previously printed expression is retained only to identify the withdrawn claim:

\begin{equation} \gamma _{\rm old}(N_{\rm params})=11.57\, N_{\rm params}^{-0.079} \quad \text{(withdrawn fit).} \tag {45} \end{equation}
46

With \(N_{\rm params}\) in individual parameters, it gives \(3.153474\) at 14M and \(1.930059\) at 7B, incompatible with the panel it was said to describe. Keeping the coefficient fixed while expressing counts in millions or billions makes these predictions larger, not smaller. No source fit, row manifest or declared alternative normalization was recovered to repair the coefficient or exponent; the accompanying \(R^2=0.41\) is therefore withdrawn too. The available E9 script concerns eight Pythia sizes, and its saved log reports zero parsed observations, not a successful 16-model fit. A new fit to an explicit panel would be a new analysis and is not silently substituted here.

8 Protocol-Specific Exponents and Derived Family Coordinates

This section distinguishes measured distance profiles, regression estimates, and quantities calculated from a fitted distribution. The initial E4 records and the October QL atlas use different acquisition and aggregation protocols. Each is analysed on its own support. Agreement between them is an empirical question, not a consequence of the finite-family identities.

8.1 Initial E4 Panel: Data and Regression Protocol

The matched uniform null for this extractor is nonflat. The 21 original rows below remain the recorded observable. Table 10 now shows the uniform null and excess slope on each row’s own grid, also supplied in the accompanying CSV. These are instrument diagnostics, not new measurements or an unbiased decomposition into learned and geometric effects. See Section 9.1 for the instrument test and its limits.

The saved records contain mean attention at sampled distances, usually with three seed means. For a declared fitting grid \(D\), we regress \(\log A(d)\) on \(\log d\) with an intercept and equal weight per distance. The slope with reversed sign is \(\widehat\gamma \). We use the exact saved grid when available. For the partial Falcon record and the two Kaggle Llama-2 records, which contain no fitting grid, the present analysis explicitly uses all saved distances \(d\ge 30\). These are recomputed estimates from those aggregates; they do not reconstruct an undocumented original fit.

The source measurement program uses sequences of length \(d+50\) at each distance, rather than one fixed context for the entire curve. Its text mode draws from the MongoDB episode corpus and its random mode generates token sequences. Complete records generally list seeds 42, 123 and 7 and a nominal prompt count of 150. The program can use a different prompt count at large distances, but that option is not recorded in the final JSON. Consequently, 150 must not be asserted as the verified count at every distance or as 150 independent prompts pooled across all seeds. The saved aggregates do not establish the exact corpus snapshot, immutable weight revision, loading precision, or correspondence of prompts between corpora.

For the 18 rows with a stored power-law estimate, the replayed exponent agrees within \(8\times 10^{-16}\). This verifies regression arithmetic on the saved inputs; it does not validate attention instrumentation or the acquisition of those inputs. No new model inference is performed. The accompanying evidence manifest maps P01–P21 to input paths and SHA-256 hashes, preserves the previous printed values, and records sensitivity to lower distance cutoffs 10, 30 and 50.

8.3 Finite-Family Quantities from the Fitted Exponents

For each full-precision fitted exponent we calculate the discrete normalizer and moments on \(d=1,\ldots ,2000\). Thus \(T_{\rm attn}=1/\widehat\gamma \), \(U=\mathbb E\log d\), \(S=\log Z_N+\widehat\gamma U\), \(I=\operatorname {Var}(\log d)\) and \(C_V=\widehat\gamma ^2I\). Extending a regression tail to this support is an additional distributional assumption. These values are neither direct attention entropies nor new measurements. In particular, the correlation of \(S\) with its input exponent does not independently validate the model. The coordinate \(\chi =1/|\widehat\gamma -1|\) is included to retain the proposed diagnostic, but it is not the finite-family Fisher susceptibility: \(I\) stays finite at one.
